name: WS2812B Addressable LED
summary: RGB LED with the controller on the die. Four pins, one data wire, and more ways to go wrong than any other four-pin part.
notes: The data threshold is 0.7 x VDD. On a 5 V strip that is 3.5 V, and a 3.3 V microcontroller does not clear it. It will often work on the bench and fail when the strip warms up. Level shift it, or drop the strip supply to about 4.3 V with a series diode so 3.3 V is enough.
A sacrificial first LED is the other standard fix: feed it 3.3 V data, run its supply from 5 V, and its DOUT comes out at a clean 5 V for the rest of the strip.
DIN and DOUT are directional and the strip is printed with arrows. Cut and solder in the wrong direction and nothing past the joint lights.
60 mA per LED at full white. A 1 m 60-LED strip is 3.6 A, which is far beyond any dev board's 5 V pin. Feed the strip directly and tie the grounds together.
300 to 500 ohm in series with DIN and 1000 uF across the supply at the head of the strip. Both are in the datasheet and both are usually skipped.
Long runs need power injected every meter or so, or the far end turns brown-red as the supply sags.

Bit timing is about 1.25 us and has no clock to resynchronize to, so an interrupt mid-frame corrupts the rest of the strip. On AVR that means interrupts off during a write; on RP2040 use PIO and on ESP32 use RMT.
SK6812 is the usual second source and adds an RGBW variant. WS2815 runs on 12 V with a backup data line so one dead LED does not kill the rest of the run.

pins.name: VDD
pins.note: 100 nF per LED, and 1000 uF bulk at the head of the strip.

pins.name: DOUT
functions: Data out to the next LED
pins.note: Reshaped 5 V output. This is what makes a sacrificial first pixel work as a level shifter.

pins.name: VSS
pins.note: Must be common with the controller's ground, even when the strip has its own supply.

pins.name: DIN
pins.note: Needs 0.7 x VDD to register. 300 to 500 ohm in series here.

circuit.title: Driving a strip

parts.why: In series with the controller's data output. Damps the edge and protects the first LED's input.
Absorbs the inrush when the whole strip lights at once.
Per LED, already on a finished strip. Only relevant if you lay out your own board.

circuit.note: Data must clear 0.7 x VDD. From a 3.3 V controller into a 5 V strip it does not, so level shift, drop the strip supply with a series diode, or sacrifice the first LED as a shifter.
